snip.t: Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Elevated JVP indicates increased right atrial pressure, common in cardiogenic pulmonary oedema.
Jugular Venous Pressure (JVP): Elevated, often with a prominent 'a' wave (right atrial contraction against a stiff RV) and sometimes a prominent 'v' wave (tricuspid regurgitation).
Haemodynamics from RHC: Higher mPAP, higher PVR, lower cardiac index, higher right atrial pressure indicate more severe disease.
Right atrial and ventricular diastolic pressures rise first due to their lower filling pressures, leading to the characteristic haemodynamic compromise.
| Echocardiography | Effusion volume and hemodynamic compromise | Anechoic fluid rim; right atrial systolic collapse and right ventricular diastolic collapse signal tamponade |

qs.q: What downstream systemic consequence directly arises from increased right atrial pressure caused by tricuspid stenosis?
o: Pulmonary venous congestion resulting in fine crackles and pulmonary edema
Systemic arterial hypertension with a wide pulse pressure and collapsing pulse
Systemic venous congestion leading to hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema
Left ventricular hypertrophy accompanied by a displaced hyperdynamic apex beat
qs.e: Increased right atrial pressure from impaired right ventricular filling causes systemic venous congestion, producing hepatomegaly, ascites, and edema. Pulmonary congestion is a feature of left-sided heart lesions.

qs.q: Which specific electrocardiographic finding is typically seen in patients with tricuspid stenosis reflecting right atrial enlargement?
o: Prolonged PR interval with widened QRS complexes and delta waves
Low voltage QRS complexes with diffuse ST-segment elevation
Deep S waves in V1 and tall R waves in V5 indicating left ventricular hypertrophy
Peaked tall P waves greater than 3mm in lead II
qs.e: Enlarged right atrium in tricuspid stenosis produces peaked tall P waves (>3mm) in lead II on an ECG. Left ventricular hypertrophy patterns are associated with aortic or mitral left-sided lesions.
